blocks.text: Electron-withdrawing groups such as a halogen atom have a negative inductive effect (-I). The halogen withdraws the bonded electrons from the carbon-carbon bond and so displays a negative inductive effect; this causes a permanent dipole in the molecule in which the halogen atom holds a negative charge and the carbon becomes partially positive (Figure 11.12). The electron-deficient C1 then pulls electrons from the C1-C2 bond, so C2 carries a smaller positive charge than C1, and the effect fades along the chain.

blocks.prompt: Define the inductive effect and contrast the effect of a methyl group with that of a chlorine atom on a neighbouring carbon (exercise Q.2a).
blocks.explanation: The inductive effect is the permanent polarisation of a sigma bond by a neighbouring atom or group. A methyl group donates electron density towards the carbon (+I), making it less positive and stabilising a carbocation there; a chlorine atom withdraws electron density (-I), leaving the carbon partially positive and a permanent dipole that weakens along the chain.

items: -I effect: a halogen withdraws sigma electrons, leaving C1 partially positive, which pulls from C2, and so on with decreasing effect; a permanent dipole.
